widget_margin.description: The Outer Margin of Widgets on the Home Page

quick_settings_height.description: How much of the screen height the quick settings panel takes. A share rather than a pixel count, so one value suits any display. A third is tight on 1080; 0.45 gives the System side room without scrolling. Clamped to 0.15-0.9.

pinned.description: The Path to your Pinned Image for the Home Background

images.description: Home Background's Path for Cycling Images

background_cycle_interval.description: The amount of time in seconds before the background cycles to a new Wallpaper

background_fade_duration.description: How long the fade animation should be when a Wallpaper cycles

output_device.description:
Where the panel plays sound.

The list is the system's own outputs - the same ones the desktop's sound settings show - read from PipeWire or PulseAudio. Default follows whatever the system is using now, which is right for most panels and wrong for one with a microphone array that takes the output as well.

Only the panel's own audio moves. Choosing one here does not change the system default, so nothing else on the machine follows it.

Without a sound server the list falls back to the sound card's own devices, which have less friendly names.

input_device.description: Which microphone the assistant listens with. 'Default' follows the system.

mic_processing.description: What the microphone does for itself. 'software' assumes a plain mic and cleans the audio here. 'hardware' is for arrays that already do it - the ReSpeaker XVF3800 and similar - and turns off the second pass, because cleaning already-clean audio is what makes speech sound underwater. Set this to hardware only if the device really does the work; on a plain mic it will hear far less.

minimum_volume.description:
The quietest the system volume is allowed to be. 0 turns this off.

A machine that picks its own output device on boot inherits whatever volume that device was left at, which is sometimes nothing - and a panel that answers silently looks broken rather than quiet.

A floor, not a level: it only ever raises the volume, so turning the panel down by hand still works down to this point. Applied when the panel starts and again whenever the wake word is heard, so a device that arrives later is caught too.

follow_bluetooth.description:
Whether a connected Bluetooth speaker becomes the system's output.

Connecting a speaker and then choosing it in the system's sound settings is two steps for something with one sensible answer. With this on, the panel makes a connected speaker the default output and moves whatever is already playing onto it, so music does not carry on out of the panel until the next track.

This changes the default for the whole machine, not just the panel - which is the point, since music plays through a browser page that follows the system default. When the speaker disconnects, the output goes back to whatever had it before.

Checked on a timer as well as on connection, so a speaker that drops and rejoins, or a sound server that restarts, is put right without anybody noticing it went wrong.

Turn this off if something else on the machine manages audio routing.

tts_enabled.description: Whether the assistant speaks its replies. Uses Kyutai Pocket TTS, which runs locally on the CPU and needs no key. A skill that would have spoken shows its answer instead when this is off.

tts_backend.description:
Which voice engine to use.

'auto' picks the best local option and 'pocket' forces it. 'deepgram' sends the text to Deepgram's Aura API and plays what comes back - that one needs an API key and spends credit per character. 'off' means the panel never speaks.

Where the voice runs is a choice inside this one, and only applies to the local engines.

tts_where.description:
Where the speaking happens.

'local' runs the voice inside the panel.
'subprocess' runs it beside the panel, on this machine.
'socket' sends the text to another machine and takes back the audio.

A neural voice holds a processor for a second or two per sentence, and inside the panel that is a second or two where the screen, the web page and the microphone all wait for it - one interpreter, one lock. Nothing can interrupt a model part way through either, so a wake word during that gap does nothing at all.

'subprocess' fixes both without needing a second machine. The work still happens here and still costs the same, but it happens somewhere the panel is not waiting on - so the screen keeps drawing, and stopping a reply becomes a message rather than a flag the model never reads. It starts on 127.0.0.1 at the port below and is restarted for you if it stops.

'socket' moves the work off this machine entirely. That one needs tts-socket-process.py running there; Packages has a download that builds it.

deepgram_api_key.description:
The Deepgram API key.

Stored in your .env file rather than here: this page renders the settings file wholesale and writes it on every save, so a key kept in it would be on screen and on disk in plain sight.

Get one from console.deepgram.com. A key that can only reach /speak works for speaking; reading the credit balance needs the management scope as well, and without it the balance simply stays blank.

deepgram_voice.description:
Which Aura voice to speak with.

The name is a whole model string - family, voice and language - because that is what the API is asked with. 'aura-2-' voices are the newer family.

This list is what the panel offers, not what your key may use. A voice the account cannot reach fails at the first reply, with the reason in the log.

tts_host.description:
The machine doing the speaking, when 'where' is socket.

An address or a name - 192.168.1.20, or desktop.local. Blank means there is nowhere to send to, and the panel will say so at startup rather than the first time it tries to speak.

tts_port.description: The port tts-socket-process.py is listening on. It defaults to 8770 at both ends, so this only needs changing if something else on that machine wanted the port.

tts_voice.description: Pocket TTS voice. 21 English, plus estelle (fr), giovanni (it), juergen (de), lola (es), rafael (pt). Overridden by Tts Voice File when that is set.

tts_language.description:
Which pretrained weights the voice uses.

Named rather than left to the model's own choice: 'default' was an option here and was not a language - the model went looking for weights by that name and would not load at all. English is what it falls back to anyway, so it is what this says.

Not every option is shipped by every version of the package. One that is not there fails at load with the list of what is, in the log.

tts_voice_file.description: A wav to clone instead of a listed voice - a local path or an hf:// URL. Overrides Tts Voice. The sample's audio quality is reproduced, so a clean recording matters more than a long one.

tts_padding_ms.description: Silence added either side of a spoken reply. The model stops when the sentence stops, so a one-line answer otherwise begins and ends hard. Also covers the moment a Bluetooth speaker takes to wake, which eats the first syllable. Pocket TTS only.

tts_rate.description: Playback speed. Pocket TTS has no rate control, so this changes the sample rate instead - which moves the PITCH with the speed. 0.95 is audibly less hurried and hard to notice; below about 0.9 it sounds like a slowed recording. Pocket TTS only.

do_not_disturb.description: Hold back notifications and every sound the panel makes. They are still written to the notification history - the point is not to be interrupted, not to lose what happened.

mute_sounds.description: Silence the panel's own sounds and its spoken replies, while leaving notifications on screen. Do not disturb implies this; this does not imply do not disturb.

notification_duration.description: How long a notification stays on screen

notification_queue_delay.description: The delay in seconds between notifications in queue

username.description: Your Username for your music API

panel_name.description: What to call this panel. Shown in Info and on the web pages this panel serves. Empty means the application name.

size.description: Set the size of the window. NOTE: this doesn't effect the actual size, its a reference

position.description: Where the window will position itself on startup

auto_lock.description: Whether the app will automatically on startup, position at X and Y, then fullscreen

interaction_timeout.description: Time of inactivity (no clicks/touches anywhere) before Client fires on_interaction_timeout. Used in the settings page to go home when no interaction has happened for a while.

check_interval.description: How often to ask GitHub whether a newer version exists. This is a single small request, not a download - nothing is fetched until you choose to update. Set to 0 to never check automatically.

restart_on_crash.description: Whether the launcher automatically restarts the app if it crashes. Turn this off to have a crash simply stop the app.

max_restart_attempts.description: How many times in a row the launcher will restart after a crash before giving up. Prevents a boot loop when something is genuinely broken.

crash_window.description: If the app ran longer than this before crashing, the restart counter resets. A long-lived session that later dies is not a boot loop.

update_grace_period.description: If a freshly-applied update crashes within this window, the launcher rolls back to the previous version and relaunches it.

mode.description: How to dim the screen. 'auto' tries real backlight control and falls back to the overlay. 'overlay' never touches the hardware. Or name one: sysfs, logind, ddcutil, brightnessctl, light.

device.description: Which display, if the machine has more than one. A name from /sys/class/backlight, or a ddcutil display number. Blank picks the first that works.

floor.description: Below this the dark overlay takes over, for monitors whose own minimum is still too bright. 0 lets the hardware cover the whole range.

enabled.description: Whether the voice assistant runs at all. Turn this off to stop the speech-to-text process entirely.

model.description:
What transcribes the phrase you said.

parakeet-v3 is NVIDIA's, run through onnx-asr. It covers 25 European languages, and unlike whisper it does not invent words out of silence - which is why nothing here has to filter its output. parakeet-v2 is English-only and slightly faster.

The weights download once on first use, after you are asked. See 'parakeet_precision' for how large that is.

parakeet_precision.description:
Which Parakeet weights to use. Ignored on the whisper models.

'int8' is 700MB, loads faster and runs faster on a panel with no GPU. 'float32' is the full-size export - 2.5GB to download and several times the memory - and is more accurate on long audio, which a phrase said to a wall panel is not. Change this and the new weights download the next time the assistant starts.

wake_word.description:
The word that wakes the assistant, spotted by openWakeWord - a model trained for the job rather than a transcription that gets read.

The list is the words openWakeWord ships models for. Anything else would need a model trained for it, which is a real piece of work and not something the panel can do.

Plugins use this as the default wake word for their skills. The assistant restarts itself when this changes.

wake_listen_timeout.description: How long the panel keeps listening after the wake word before giving up. Too short and it stops mid-thought; too long and it sits listening to the room.

max_phrase_seconds.description: The longest a single phrase may run before it is thrown away and the panel stands down. Speech that goes on past this is a television or a conversation in the room rather than a question, and transcribing it hands whole sentences of it to the skills.

session_silence.description: How long a pause ends your sentence once the assistant is in a conversation. Lower reacts faster; too low and a breath mid-sentence is treated as the end, which splits one question into several and sends each of them separately. 800ms suits normal speech.

wake_sensitivity.description:
How sure openWakeWord has to be before it counts as the wake word.

0.5 is the library's own suggestion. LOWER hears the word through more noise - a fan, music, a room away - and also fires on more things that were not it. HIGHER wants a clearer say of it and misses more.

Worth moving in steps of 0.05 and living with for a day: the cost of going too low is the panel waking up on its own, which is more annoying than saying the word twice. The assistant restarts itself when this changes.

wake_sensitivity_speaking.description:
The same bar, for the moment the panel is talking. 0 means use the ordinary sensitivity above.

While a reply is being read out the microphone carries the panel's own voice alongside yours, so the wake word arrives buried in a way it never is in a quiet room - and the setting that works for the room is often too high for this.

Going lower costs less here than it does elsewhere: a false fire only interrupts a sentence the panel was already reading out. Try 0.05 below the ordinary one and keep going while it still refuses to be interrupted. The assistant restarts itself when this changes.

wake_noise_suppression.description:
Clean the audio before the wake word is looked for.

Uses SpeexDSP, which is aimed at steady background noise - a fan, an in-window air conditioner, a fridge. Exactly the sort that never stops and sits under everything said in the room.

Off by default because it costs a little per frame and because a microphone that already does this in hardware - a beamforming array - does not want it done twice.

Needs speexdsp-ns installed. Without it the panel says so once and carries on.

wake_speech_gate.description:
Refuse a wake unless the same moment also sounded like speech.

0 is off. Around 0.5 is a reasonable start.

A second, separate model decides whether a frame contains a voice at all, and the wake word is only accepted if it agrees. That does nothing about somebody on television saying the word, and a great deal about a clatter or a door that happens to score highly.

It asks something of the audio the wake word alone does not, so set it gently: too high and a real wake said quietly is refused, with nothing on screen to say why.

wake_diagnostics.description: Explain every wake in the log: how sure the spotter was, and a transcript of what was being said around it. Turn this on to find out what has been waking the panel, and off again afterwards - it runs the speech model an extra time on every wake.

wake_report.description:
Keep a wake word report in logs/wake.log, and a page that summarises it.

Wake word trouble is two symptoms with one cause. Firing at the television and missing you over a fan look like opposite problems and are usually the same one - the word arrived buried, and no sensitivity has a good setting any more. Telling them apart needs numbers from the room it happens in.

The report records what the microphone is and which channel was taken, how loud the room is, every wake, and every NEAR MISS - a say of the word that scored something but not enough. That last one is the half a log has never had: 0.45 against a bar of 0.50 and 0.02 against the same bar both look like nothing happening, and they are completely different faults.

Near misses are transcribed so you can see what it heard instead, at most six a minute.

wake_ignore_similarity.description:
How alike a wake has to be to a sound already learned as noise before it is passed over.

1.0 is the same sound twice. Unrelated sounds sit far below this.

The two mistakes do not cost the same. Set too high, a television wakes the panel again and the wake shows up in the report. Set too low, the panel silently ignores you saying the wake word properly, and nothing on screen says why - so this errs high.

Every wake records how close it came to the nearest learned sound, whether or not it was passed over, so the Wake report shows the spread before you move this.

gate_unaddressed.description:
Whether a phrase that matched no skill has to look like it was said to the panel before it reaches the AI fallback.

A wake word fires on television audio often enough that something has to decide what to do with what follows, and without this the answer is always "ask the AI" - so the panel answers the room out loud. With it on, an utterance shaped like conversation rather than a request is dropped and logged.

Biased toward dropping: an utterance with no signal either way goes too. A missed request costs saying it again; a phantom interaction costs a panel talking over what you were watching. Turn this off if the log shows it dropping things you meant.

voice_bar.description: Show the thin activity bar along the bottom of the screen while the assistant is listening.

voice_bar_hold.description: Minimum time the activity bar keeps a transcript on screen. Longer transcripts are held longer than this automatically.

greet_on_start.description: Whether the assistant says hello out loud when it starts listening. The notification appears either way; this is only whether it is spoken. Off by default - a panel that restarts itself at four in the morning should not announce it.

enabled.description: Developer controls and extra logging. Plugins may add their own switches while this is on.
